stack.body:
You already know this structure from the canteen, and the ideas carry over exactly. Think of a stack of plates in a canteen. You add a plate on top and take a plate from the top; to reach the plate at the bottom you must remove everything above it. A stack behaves exactly like this: insertion and removal happen at one end only, the top. The operations are push (add on top), pop (remove and return the top), peek or top (read the top without removing) and isEmpty. The last item pushed is the first popped — LIFO, last in, first out.

As an ADT, a stack is only this contract. Two implementations are common. In an array, an integer top records the index of the top element (−1 when empty); push increments it and stores, pop returns and decrements. The size is fixed, so pushing onto a full stack is overflow and must be checked, as must underflow (popping an empty stack). In a linked list, push inserts a new node at the head and pop removes the head — no size limit apart from memory. Both give O(1) for every operation, which is the stack’s selling point. C++ provides std::stack built on a deque; the program below pushes 10, 20, 30, 40 and pops them back in reverse order.

Which end of the stack do you touch to read the most recent item? That single answer is the whole contract.
keynotes: A stack allows insertion and removal at one end only, the top, so the last item pushed is the first popped: LIFO.
The operations are push, pop, peek (top) and isEmpty.
As an ADT a stack is only this contract, and there are two common implementations.

apps.body:
Whenever something must be undone in reverse order, a stack quietly appears, and you use one every day. Whenever something must be undone in reverse order, a stack appears. The undo command in an editor pushes each action and pops it to reverse. A web browser’s back button is a stack of visited pages. The run-time system uses a stack for function calls — each call pushes a frame holding its parameters, local variables and return address, and each return pops it — which is the subject of the recursion sections below. Compilers use stacks to check balanced brackets, to convert and evaluate expressions, and to parse nested constructs. Algorithms use them to simulate recursion (depth-first search) and for backtracking (maze solving).

The bracket-matching algorithm is the cleanest first example. Scan the text left to right; on an opening bracket (, [ or { push it; on a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opening bracket — pop it; any mismatch is an error; at the end the stack must be empty. Run it on {[()]}(: the first six characters match perfectly, but the final “(” is never closed, so the stack is not empty and the text is not balanced.

Can you think of another everyday feature that works like “undo”? It is probably a stack too.
keynotes: Undo in an editor pushes each action and pops it to reverse; the browser back button is a stack of visited pages.
The run-time system uses a stack for function calls, each call pushing a frame with parameters, local variables and return address.
Compilers use stacks to check balanced brackets and to convert and evaluate expressions.

postfix.body:
Here is a small piece of magic for you: a way to write arithmetic that needs no brackets at all. You will see that precedence, which you have used since school, can disappear completely once the operators are placed after their operands. We normally write arithmetic in infix notation, with the operator between its operands: A + B. It is ambiguous without rules — what does A + B × C mean? — so we need precedence (× before +), associativity (left to right for − and /; right to left for exponentiation) and parentheses to override them. In postfix (reverse Polish, Łukasiewicz in reverse) the operator follows its operands: A B +. In prefix (Polish) it precedes them: + A B. Both are unambiguous without parentheses or precedence, because the position of each operator already says what it applies to. That makes them ideal for a machine, and a stack evaluates them effortlessly.

Evaluating postfix is mechanical: scan left to right; push each operand; on an operator, pop the top two values (the first popped is the right operand), apply the operator, push the result. At the end the stack holds the answer. For 2 3 * 5 4 * + 9 −: push 2, 3; × gives 6; push 5, 4; × gives 20; + gives 26… the run below computes 6 + 20 − 9 = 17.

Converting infix to postfix (Dijkstra’s shunting-yard algorithm) uses a stack of operators. Read tokens left to right. An operand goes straight to the output. For an operator, pop and output any stacked operator of higher or equal precedence (for left-associative operators), then push it. “(” is pushed; “)” pops and outputs until the matching “(” (which is discarded). At the end pop everything to the output. A + B × C − (D / E) becomes A B C * + D E / -. Step the card: the stack is the lower row, the output the row above.

Try writing (A + B) × C in postfix yourself, then evaluate it with a stack of numbers. Notice how the order of the operators in the postfix string is exactly the order in which the work will be done.
keynotes: Infix writes the operator between its operands (A + B) and needs precedence, associativity and parentheses.
Postfix (A B +) and prefix (+ A B) are unambiguous without parentheses or precedence.
A stack of numbers evaluates postfix; a stack of operators converts infix to postfix.

rec.body:
Some problems contain a smaller copy of themselves, like a set of Russian dolls, and recursion is the tool for them. Take your time here, because almost every later chapter, from trees to sorting, depends on you being comfortable with this idea. Some problems contain smaller copies of themselves. To compute n!, note that n! = n × (n − 1)!: the factorial of n is n times the factorial of something smaller. A recursive function exploits this by calling itself on the smaller problem. Every correct recursive function has two parts: a base case that is answered directly (0! = 1) and stops the recursion, and a recursive case that reduces the problem and calls the function again, moving towards the base case. Leave out the base case, or fail to approach it, and the calls never stop.

How does the machine keep track? Each call gets its own activation record (stack frame) on the call stack, holding its parameters, its local variables and where to return. A new call pushes a frame; a return pops it. The run-time stack is the stack ADT of the previous sections, used by the machine itself. That is why a recursion that goes a million levels deep crashes with a stack overflow: it has run out of frame space. Run the factorial program and watch the stack grow five frames deep, then unwind as each pending multiplication completes.

Trace the figure: fact(4) calls fact(3), which calls fact(2), then fact(1) — the base case, which returns 1 without calling anything. Now the frames pop in reverse order: fact(2) returns 2 × 1 = 2, fact(3) returns 3 × 2 = 6, fact(4) returns 4 × 6 = 24. Nothing is multiplied on the way down; all the work happens on the way back up.

What would happen to n! if you forgot the base case? Picture the calls piling up. Then trace n! for n = 3 by hand and watch each call wait for the one below it.
keynotes: n! = n × (n − 1)!, so a recursive function calls itself on the smaller problem.
Every correct recursive function has a base case, such as 0! = 1, and a recursive case that moves towards it.
Leaving out the base case, or failing to approach it, makes the recursion run until the stack overflows.

examples.body:
Four short programs teach most of what exams ask, so let’s walk through them one by one, and you can follow along. Four short programs teach most of what exams ask. Greatest common divisor (Euclid): gcd(a, b) = a if b = 0, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b). Each call shrinks the second argument, so it must reach 0. gcd(48, 18) → gcd(18, 12) → gcd(12, 6) → gcd(6, 0) = 6. Digit sum: sumDigits(n) = n if n < 10 else (n mod 10) + sumDigits(n / 10); 9045 gives 5 + 4 + 0 + 9 = 18. Fast exponentiation: x^n = (x^{n/2})² for even n and x·(x^{n/2})² for odd n — halving the exponent gives O(log n) multiplications instead of n; power(2, 10) needs only 5 calls. Binary search (next chapters) is the same halving idea on a sorted array.

Compare fast exponentiation with the obvious loop. Computing 2¹⁰ naively takes 10 multiplications; the recursive halving version takes five calls (n = 10, 5, 2, 1, 0). For exponent a million that is 1,000,000 against about 20: the difference between a design that works and one that does not.

Trace gcd(48, 18) yourself on paper before checking the chain of calls above.
keynotes: Euclid’s gcd(a, b) is a if b = 0, otherwise gcd(b, a mod b); gcd(48, 18) reaches 6.
The digit sum of 9045 is 5 + 4 + 0 + 9 = 18.
Fast exponentiation halves the exponent, giving O(log n) multiplications instead of n.

hanoi.body:
This puzzle looks impossible when you try it by hand, and trivial once you think recursively; you will see why. Three pegs, A, B and C. Peg A holds n disks of decreasing size, the largest at the bottom. Move them all to C, one at a time, never placing a larger disk on a smaller one, using B as a spare. Try it by hand with n = 4 and you will be lost; think recursively and it is trivial. To move n disks from A to C: first move the top n − 1 disks from A to B (using C as the spare), then move the largest disk from A to C, then move the n − 1 disks from B to C (using A). The two sub-moves are the same problem with one disk fewer. The base case is zero disks: do nothing.

Counting the moves gives a recurrence. Let T(n) be the number of moves. Then T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1 + T(n − 1) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 with T(0) = 0. Unrolling shows T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1: T(1) = 1, T(2) = 3, T(3) = 7, T(4) = 15. The cost is exponential — adding a single disk doubles the work — and it is provably the minimum number of moves, so no cleverness avoids it. The legend says monks move 64 golden disks; at one move a second that is 2⁶⁴ − 1 seconds, about 585 billion years.

Say aloud the three moves for n disks. Notice that the two sub-problems are the same puzzle with one disk fewer.
keynotes: To move n disks from A to C, first move n − 1 disks to B, then move the largest disk to C, then move the n − 1 disks from B to C.
The two sub-moves are the same problem with one disk fewer.
The total number of moves is 2ⁿ − 1.

types.body:
Recursion comes in several shapes, and the shape tells you how expensive it will be. Recursion comes in several shapes. In direct recursion a function calls itself; in indirect (mutual) recursion f calls g and g calls f. In linear recursion each call makes at most one further call (factorial, gcd); in binary or tree recursion each makes two (Fibonacci, Hanoi), which is where exponential costs hide. A call is tail recursive if the recursive call is the very last thing the function does — there is nothing left to do after it returns, such as the multiplication in n * fact(n-1). A tail-recursive function can be turned into a loop automatically (tail-call optimisation) so it uses no extra stack; the factorial above is not tail recursive, but the accumulator version fact(n, acc) = fact(n − 1, n·acc) is.

The costs of recursion are time (call overhead) and space (a frame per pending call, O(depth)). The danger is repeated work. The naive Fibonacci function recomputes the same values over and over: fib(10) makes 177 calls for an answer that needs only 10 additions. Remember the answers in a table — memoisation — and each value is computed once; fib(10) then makes only 19 calls. This is the seed of dynamic programming: when subproblems overlap, recursion needs a memory.

Is the factorial function tail recursive? Check whether anything is left to do after the call returns.
keynotes: Direct recursion calls itself while indirect (mutual) recursion has f call g and g call f.
Linear recursion makes at most one further call, while binary or tree recursion makes two, which is where exponential costs hide.
A call is tail recursive if it is the very last thing the function does.

iter.body:
So which should you use, a loop or recursion? The honest answer depends on the problem, and here is how to choose. Anything recursive can be written with a loop and an explicit stack, because the call stack is a stack; and any loop can be written as tail recursion. Which to use? Recursion is natural when the problem or the data is recursive — trees, divide-and-conquer, backtracking — and the code mirrors the definition. Iteration is usually faster and uses O(1) stack, and is safer for very deep problems. A good rule: use recursion when it makes the algorithm clearer and the depth is modest (log n or at most a few thousand); use a loop when the recursion is linear and the depth could be large.

Backtracking is recursion with an undo step. To solve a puzzle (eight queens, a maze, sudoku) you make a choice, recurse to try to complete the solution, and if you reach a dead end you undo the choice and try the next. The recursion stack remembers where to back up to. The same idea explains depth-first search in graphs, which we use two chapters from now.

Think of a tree walk and a simple sum. Which would you write recursively, and which with a loop?
keynotes: Anything recursive can be written with a loop and an explicit stack, and any loop can be written as tail recursion.
Recursion is natural for recursive problems or data such as trees, divide-and-conquer and backtracking.
Iteration is usually faster and uses O(1) stack.

summary.body:
Time to gather the chapter in a few lines, and you can use them as your checklist.

  • A stack is LIFO with O(1) push, pop and peek; check overflow and underflow. It powers undo, back, bracket matching, expression handling and the call stack.
  • Postfix needs no parentheses: evaluate with a stack of numbers; convert from infix with a stack of operators (shunting-yard).
  • Recursion = base case + a smaller problem; each active call has a stack frame; work happens as frames return.
  • Classics: factorial, gcd (Euclid), digit sum, fast exponentiation (log n), Hanoi (2ⁿ − 1 moves).
  • Tree recursion can be exponential (naive Fibonacci); memoisation fixes it. Tail recursion can become a loop. Backtracking is recursion with undo.

Cover the bullets and recite them. Which one did you miss?
keynotes: A stack is LIFO with O(1) push, pop and peek, and powers undo, back, bracket matching, expression handling and the call stack.
Postfix needs no parentheses: evaluate with a stack of numbers and convert from infix with a stack of operators.
Recursion is a base case plus a smaller problem, and Hanoi takes 2ⁿ − 1 moves.
